claim: Rhodopsin is the most abundant outer segment protein.
source: Rhodopsin is the most abundant outer segment protein and its proper transport is essential for formation of this organelle, suggesting that such a dependency might exist.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Rhodopsin's proper transport is essential for formation of the outer segment organelle.
source: Rhodopsin is the most abundant outer segment protein and its proper transport is essential for formation of this organelle, suggesting that such a dependency might exist.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Guanylate cyclase-1 requires rhodopsin for intracellular stability.
source: Indeed, we demonstrated that guanylate cyclase-1, producing the cGMP second messenger in photoreceptors, requires rhodopsin for intracellular stability and outer segment delivery.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experiments shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Guanylate cyclase-1 requires rhodopsin for outer segment delivery.
source: Indeed, we demonstrated that guanylate cyclase-1, producing the cGMP second messenger in photoreceptors, requires rhodopsin for intracellular stability and outer segment delivery.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experiments shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Guanylate cyclase-1 is a novel rhodopsin-binding protein.
source: We elucidated this dependency by showing that guanylate cyclase-1 is a novel rhodopsin-binding protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Guanylate cyclase-1 produces the cGMP second messenger in photoreceptors.
source: Indeed, we demonstrated that guanylate cyclase-1, producing the cGMP second messenger in photoreceptors, requires rhodopsin for intracellular stability and outer segment delivery.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GC-1 function.

claim: Outer segments serve as a nearly unmatched model system for studying general principles of GPCR signaling.
source: Such a distinct functional and morphological specialization allow outer segments to serve as a nearly unmatched model system for studying general principles of GPCR signaling (Arshavsky et al., 2002) and, in more recent years, a model for ciliary trafficking (Garcia-Gonzalo and Reiter, 2012; Nemet et al., 2015; Pearring et al., 2013; Schou et al., 2015; Wang and Deretic, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Outer segments serve as a model for ciliary trafficking.
source: Such a distinct functional and morphological specialization allow outer segments to serve as a nearly unmatched model system for studying general principles of GPCR signaling (Arshavsky et al., 2002) and, in more recent years, a model for ciliary trafficking (Garcia-Gonzalo and Reiter, 2012; Nemet et al., 2015; Pearring et al., 2013; Schou et al., 2015; Wang and Deretic, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Nearly all mechanistic studies of outer segment protein trafficking have been devoted to rhodopsin.
source: Indeed, nearly all mechanistic studies of outer segment protein trafficking have been devoted to rhodopsin (Nemet et al., 2015; Wang and Deretic, 2014), which is a GPCR visual pigment comprising the majority of the outer segment membrane protein mass (Palczewski, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous reviews.

claim: Rhodopsin is a GPCR visual pigment comprising the majority of the outer segment membrane protein mass.
source: Indeed, nearly all mechanistic studies of outer segment protein trafficking have been devoted to rhodopsin (Nemet et al., 2015; Wang and Deretic, 2014), which is a GPCR visual pigment comprising the majority of the outer segment membrane protein mass (Palczewski, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for outer segment delivery of transmembrane proteins other than rhodopsin remain essentially unknown.
source: The mechanisms responsible for outer segment delivery of other transmembrane proteins remain essentially unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Some outer segment proteins contain short outer segment targeting signals that can be identified through site-specific mutagenesis.
source: Some of them contain short outer segment targeting signals, which can be identified through site-specific mutagenesis (Deretic et al., 1998; Li et al., 1996; Pearring et al., 2014; Salinas et al., 2013; Sung et al., 1994; Tam et al., 2000; 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Retinal guanylate cyclase 1 (GC-1) is an exception that lacks a distinct outer segment targeting motif despite exhaustive mutagenesis.
source: A documented exception is retinal guanylate cyclase 1 (GC-1), whose exhaustive mutagenesis did not yield a distinct outer segment targeting motif (Karan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GC-1 is a critical component of the phototransduction machinery responsible for synthesizing the second messenger, cGMP.
source: GC-1 is a critical component of the phototransduction machinery responsible for synthesizing the second messenger, cGMP (Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GC-1 is the only guanylate cyclase isoform expressed in the outer segments of cones.
source: GC-1 is the only guanylate cyclase isoform expressed in the outer segments of cones and the predominant isoform in rods (Baehr et al., 2007; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GC-1 is the predominant guanylate cyclase isoform in rods.
source: GC-1 is the only guanylate cyclase isoform expressed in the outer segments of cones and the predominant isoform in rods (Baehr et al., 2007; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GC-1 knockout in mice is characterized by severe degeneration of cones.
source: GC-1 knockout in mice is characterized by severe degeneration of cones and abnormal light-response recovery kinetics in rods (Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GC-1 knockout in mice is characterized by abnormal light-response recovery kinetics in rods.
source: GC-1 knockout in mice is characterized by severe degeneration of cones and abnormal light-response recovery kinetics in rods (Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A very large number of GC-1 mutations found in human patients causes one of the most severe forms of early onset retinal dystrophy, called Leber's congenital amaurosis.
source: Furthermore, a very large number of GC-1 mutations found in human patients causes one of the most severe forms of early onset retinal dystrophy, called Leber's congenital amaurosis (Boye, 2014; Kitiratschky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Many GC-1 mutations causing Leber's congenital amaurosis are located outside the catalytic site of GC-1.
source: Many of these mutations are located outside the catalytic site of GC-1, which raises great interest in understanding the mechanisms of its intracellular processing and trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from clinical genetics.

claim: Normal outer segments are cylindrical structures filled with an ordered stack of several hundred membrane discs.
source: Normal outer segments are cylindrical structures filled with an ordered stack of several hundred membrane discs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in electron micrographs in Figure 1A and is established knowledge.

claim: Rho-/- rods only develop small ciliary extensions filled with disorganized membrane material.
source: In contrast, Rho-/- rods only develop small ciliary extensions filled with disorganized membrane material (Figure 1A; Humphries et al., 1997; Lee et al., 2006; Lem et al., 1999).
evidence: This is shown in electron micrographs in Figure 1A and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Peripherin reliably targets to the ciliary extension in Rho-/- rods despite the morphological defect.
source: Despite this morphological defect, two outer segment-specific proteins, peripherin and R9AP, have been previously shown to reliably target to this ciliary extension (Lee et al., 2006; Pearring et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: R9AP reliably targets to the ciliary extension in Rho-/- rods despite the morphological defect.
source: Despite this morphological defect, two outer segment-specific proteins, peripherin and R9AP, have been previously shown to reliably target to this ciliary extension (Lee et al., 2006; Pearring et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rom-1 localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ABCA4 localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GC-2 localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CNGα1 localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CNGβ1 localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Protocadherin 21 localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Prominin localizes specifically to the ciliary extensions of Rho-/- rods.
source: Remarkably, nine out of ten proteins were localized specifically to the ciliary extensions of the Rho-/- rods. They included Rom1, ABCA4, GC-2, CNGα1, CNGβ1, protocadherin 21, and prominin (Figure 1B–H), as well as previously reported R9AP and peripherin (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GC-1 displayed a punctate pattern in the outer segment layer with no distinct signal in rod ciliary extensions of Rho-/- mice.
source: A striking exception was GC-1, which displayed a punctate pattern in the outer segment layer with no distinct signal in rod ciliary extensions (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The GC-1-positive puncta in Rho-/- mice corresponds to cone outer segments.
source: Further analysis using a cone marker, peanut agglutinin, revealed that the GC-1-positive puncta corresponds to cone outer segments (Figure 1L; note that cone outer segments in Rho-/- mice are smaller than normal).
evidence: This is demonstrated by double labeling shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Cone outer segments in Rho-/- mice are smaller than normal.
source: Further analysis using a cone marker, peanut agglutinin, revealed that the GC-1-positive puncta corresponds to cone outer segments (Figure 1L; note that cone outer segments in Rho-/- mice are smaller than normal).
evidence: This is noted as an observation from Figure 1L.

claim: Faint fluorescent signal for GC-1 outside the cone outer segments in Rho-/- mice was indistinguishable from non-specific background in the outer segment layer of GC-1 knockout mice.
source: Faint fluorescent signal outside the cone outer segments was indistinguishable from non-specific background in the outer segment layer of GC-1 knockout mice (Gucy2e-/-; Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with GC-1 knockout controls shown in Figure 2.

claim: The knockout of GC-1 was not associated with reduction or mislocalization of rhodopsin from rod outer segments.
source: As documented in a previous study (Baehr et al., 2007), the knockout of GC-1 was not associated with reduction or mislocalization of rhodopsin from rod outer segments (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2 and supported by a citation.

claim: Proteins retaining their normal outer segment localization in Rho-/- mice were all expressed at 40–80% WT levels.
source: We found that proteins retaining their normal outer segment localization (Figure 1) were all expressed at 40–80% WT levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative Western blotting shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GC-1 content in Rho-/- retinas was only 10 ± 3% (SEM, n=5) of WT.
source: Once again the outlier was GC-1 whose content in Rho-/- retinas was only 10 ± 3% (SEM, n=5) of WT (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative Western blotting shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: GC-1 in Rho-/- rods is reduced by at least 95%.
source: Considering that (1) a large fraction of this GC-1 is expressed in cones (Figure 1L); (2) cones comprise 3% of mouse photoreceptors; and (3) cones express more GC-1 than rods (Dizhoor et al., 1994), our most conservative estimate is that GC-1 in Rho-/- rods is reduced by at least 95%.
evidence: This is calculated from the Western blot data combined with known facts about cone/rod ratios and GC-1 expression patterns.

claim: Cones comprise 3% of mouse photoreceptors.
source: Considering that (1) a large fraction of this GC-1 is expressed in cones (Figure 1L); (2) cones comprise 3% of mouse photoreceptors; and (3) cones express more GC-1 than rods (Dizhoor et al., 1994), our most conservative estimate is that GC-1 in Rho-/- rods is reduced by at least 95%.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mouse retinal composition.

claim: Cones express more GC-1 than rods.
source: Considering that (1) a large fraction of this GC-1 is expressed in cones (Figure 1L); (2) cones comprise 3% of mouse photoreceptors; and (3) cones express more GC-1 than rods (Dizhoor et al., 1994), our most conservative estimate is that GC-1 in Rho-/- rods is reduced by at least 95%.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The reduction of GC-1 in Rho-/- mice is not caused by a loss of the GC-1 transcript.
source: This reduction is not caused by a loss of the GC-1 transcript, since qRT-PCR showed that the amount of GC-1 mRNA in Rho-/- retinas was actually twice higher than in WT retinas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), perhaps reflecting a feedback mechanism attempting to compensate for the missing GC-1 enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amount of GC-1 mRNA in Rho-/- retinas was actually twice higher than in WT retinas.
source: This reduction is not caused by a loss of the GC-1 transcript, since qRT-PCR showed that the amount of GC-1 mRNA in Rho-/- retinas was actually twice higher than in WT retinas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), perhaps reflecting a feedback mechanism attempting to compensate for the missing GC-1 enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increased GC-1 mRNA in Rho-/- retinas may reflect a feedback mechanism attempting to compensate for the missing GC-1 enzyme.
source: This reduction is not caused by a loss of the GC-1 transcript, since qRT-PCR showed that the amount of GC-1 mRNA in Rho-/- retinas was actually twice higher than in WT retinas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), perhaps reflecting a feedback mechanism attempting to compensate for the missing GC-1 enzyme.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the observed increase in mRNA.

claim: GC-1 is unique among outer segment transmembrane proteins in its reliance on rhodopsin for intracellular stability and outer segment localization.
source: Taken together, the data reported in Figures 1 and 3 demonstrate that GC-1 is unique among outer segment transmembrane proteins in its reliance on rhodopsin for intracellular stability and outer segment localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The outer segment localization of rhodopsin relies on its C-terminal sequence including the VXPX targeting motif.
source: The outer segment localization of rhodopsin relies on its C-terminal sequence (including the VXPX targeting motif), which is both necessary and sufficient for rhodopsin delivery (Deretic et al., 1998; Li et al., 1996; Sung et al., 1994; Tam et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Rhodopsin's C-terminal sequence is both necessary and sufficient for rhodopsin delivery to the outer segment.
source: The outer segment localization of rhodopsin relies on its C-terminal sequence (including the VXPX targeting motif), which is both necessary and sufficient for rhodopsin delivery (Deretic et al., 1998; Li et al., 1996; Sung et al., 1994; Tam et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Adding rhodopsin's C-terminal sequence to other proteins enables their specific outer segment trafficking.
source: Taking advantage of the fact that adding this sequence to other proteins enables their specific outer segment trafficking (Tam et al., 2000; reviewed in Pearring et al., 2013), we used chimeric proteins to address this question.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Full-length Htr6 robustly expresses and reliably targets to rod outer segments of WT and Rho-/- mice.
source: Although this receptor is not endogenous to rods, we found that both full-length Htr6 and its rhodopsin chimeras robustly express and reliably target to rod outer segments of WT and Rho-/- mice. This is shown in Figure 4, where these constructs were introduced into rods by the technique of in vivo electroporation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Rhodopsin chimeras with Htr6 robustly express and reliably target to rod outer segments of WT and Rho-/- mice.
source: Although this receptor is not endogenous to rods, we found that both full-length Htr6 and its rhodopsin chimeras robustly express and reliably target to rod outer segments of WT and Rho-/- mice. This is shown in Figure 4, where these constructs were introduced into rods by the technique of in vivo electroporation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Htr6 did not restore GC-1 content in outer segments of Rho-/- rods despite its strong expression.
source: Despite its strong expression in outer segments of Rho-/- rods, Htr6 did not restore their GC-1 content (Figure 4A) and neither did the chimera containing the Htr6 seven-helical core fused to rhodopsin's C-terminus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The chimera containing the Htr6 seven-helical core fused to rhodopsin's C-terminus did not restore GC-1 content in outer segments of Rho-/- rods.
source: Despite its strong expression in outer segments of Rho-/- rods, Htr6 did not restore their GC-1 content (Figure 4A) and neither did the chimera containing the Htr6 seven-helical core fused to rhodopsin's C-terminus (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of the chimera containing rhodopsin's core fused to Htr6's C-terminus restored GC-1 in the outer segments of transfected Rho-/- rods.
source: In contrast, expression of the chimera containing rhodopsin's core fused to Htr6's C-terminus did restore GC-1 in the outer segments of transfected rods (Figure 4C), as efficiently as rhodopsin (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of full-length rhodopsin restored GC-1 in the outer segments of transfected Rho-/- rods.
source: In contrast, expression of the chimera containing rhodopsin's core fused to Htr6's C-terminus did restore GC-1 in the outer segments of transfected rods (Figure 4C), as efficiently as rhodopsin (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both intracellular stability and outer segment delivery of GC-1 rely directly on rhodopsin and not on the activity of the ciliary trafficking pathway driven by rhodopsin's C-terminus.
source: Therefore, both intracellular stability and outer segment delivery of GC-1 rely directly on rhodopsin and not on the activity of the ciliary trafficking pathway driven by rhodopsin's C-terminus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: A large fraction of GC-1 can be co-precipitated with rhodopsin using the monoclonal anti-rhodopsin antibody 1D4.
source: The experiment in Figure 5A demonstrates that a large fraction of GC-1 can be co-precipitated with rhodopsin using the monoclonal anti-rhodopsin antibody 1D4.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neither rhodopsin nor GC-1 was precipitated when 1D4 was replaced with non-immune mouse IgG.
source: The specificity of this co-precipitation was established by replacing 1D4 with non-immune mouse IgG and by performing the experiment in the presence of the 1D4 epitope-blocking peptide (Hodges et al., 1988). Neither rhodopsin nor GC-1 was precipitated under these conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neither rhodopsin nor GC-1 was precipitated when the experiment was performed in the presence of the 1D4 epitope-blocking peptide.
source: The specificity of this co-precipitation was established by replacing 1D4 with non-immune mouse IgG and by performing the experiment in the presence of the 1D4 epitope-blocking peptide (Hodges et al., 1988). Neither rhodopsin nor GC-1 was precipitated under these conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 5A and supported by a citation.

claim: DnaJB6 did not precipitate with the rhodopsin-GC-1 complex.
source: We also probed the 1D4 precipitate for the chaperone protein, DnaJB6 (Figure 5A), which was previously shown to link GC-1 to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) particle for ciliary transport (Bhowmick et al., 2009). Whereas a strong DnaJB6 staining was identified in the retinal lysate, it did not precipitate with the rhodopsin-GC-1 complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DnaJB6 was previously shown to link GC-1 to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) particle for ciliary transport.
source: We also probed the 1D4 precipitate for the chaperone protein, DnaJB6 (Figure 5A), which was previously shown to link GC-1 to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) particle for ciliary transport (Bhowmick et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The GC-1 interaction with DnaJB6 is transient.
source: This suggests that, unlike the interaction with rhodopsin, the GC-1 interaction with DnaJB6 is transient.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure to co-precipitate DnaJB6 with the rhodopsin-GC-1 complex.

claim: No appreciable fraction of peripherin was found in the rhodopsin precipitate under the experimental conditions used.
source: Following a recent report that another rhodopsin-binding protein is peripherin (Becirovic et al., 2014), we also probed the rhodopsin precipitate for peripherin. However, no appreciable fraction of peripherin was found in precipitate, both under our experimental conditions and in membranes dissolved in Triton X-100 as in their study.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Peripherin was reported to be a rhodopsin-binding protein.
source: Following a recent report that another rhodopsin-binding protein is peripherin (Becirovic et al., 2014), we also probed the rhodopsin precipitate for peripherin.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is highly unlikely that rhodopsin's interaction with peripherin could be as prominent as that with GC-1.
source: Given that these authors did not show what fraction of total peripherin was precipitating with rhodopsin in their assays, it is hard to fully reconcile these observations, although it is highly unlikely that rhodopsin's interaction with peripherin could be as prominent as that with GC-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of co-precipitation efficiencies.

claim: The efficiency of GC-1 co-precipitation with rhodopsin was highly dependent on the type and concentration of detergent used for membrane solubilization.
source: Importantly, the efficiency of GC-1 co-precipitation with rhodopsin was highly dependent on the type and concentration of detergent used for membrane solubilization. The co-precipitated fraction of GC-1 diminished when we increased the concentration of dodecyl maltoside, or used Triton X-100 instead (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The co-precipitated fraction of GC-1 diminished when the concentration of dodecyl maltoside was increased.
source: Importantly, the efficiency of GC-1 co-precipitation with rhodopsin was highly dependent on the type and concentration of detergent used for membrane solubilization. The co-precipitated fraction of GC-1 diminished when we increased the concentration of dodecyl maltoside, or used Triton X-100 instead (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The co-precipitated fraction of GC-1 diminished when Triton X-100 was used instead of dodecyl maltoside.
source: Importantly, the efficiency of GC-1 co-precipitation with rhodopsin was highly dependent on the type and concentration of detergent used for membrane solubilization. The co-precipitated fraction of GC-1 diminished when we increased the concentration of dodecyl maltoside, or used Triton X-100 instead (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Instability of membrane protein complexes in detergent solutions is a common phenomenon.
source: Such instability of membrane protein complexes in detergent solutions is a common phenomenon (Prive, 2007), and we believe that this likely hindered identification of GC-1's interaction with rhodopsin in the past.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The instability of the rhodopsin-GC-1 complex in detergent solutions likely hindered identification of GC-1's interaction with rhodopsin in the past.
source: Such instability of membrane protein complexes in detergent solutions is a common phenomenon (Prive, 2007), and we believe that this likely hindered identification of GC-1's interaction with rhodopsin in the past.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed detergent sensitivity.

claim: Rhodopsin in mouse rods is expressed at a 1400-fold molar excess over GC-1.
source: The challenge of this experiment was that rhodopsin in mouse rods is expressed at a 1400-fold molar excess over GC-1 (Peshenko et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The theoretical limit of rhodopsin bound to GC-1 is only 0.07% of its total amount.
source: Therefore, the theoretical limit of rhodopsin bound to GC-1 is only 0.07% of its total amount, and its detection requires special measures to reduce non-specific rhodopsin binding to the beads.
evidence: This is calculated from the known molar ratio between rhodopsin and GC-1.

claim: Rho+/- mice express twice less rhodopsin without affecting the amounts of other outer segment proteins.
source: First, we improved the molar ratio between GC-1 and rhodopsin by using retinal lysates from Rho+/- mice, which express twice less rhodopsin without affecting the amounts of other outer segment proteins (Calvert et al., 2001; Liang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rhodopsin precipitation with anti-GC-1 antibody exceeded non-specific background with non-immune IgG by over six-fold.
source: Under these conditions, rhodopsin precipitation with anti-GC-1 antibody exceeded non-specific background with non-immune IgG by over six-fold (6.5 ± 1.7, n=3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rhodopsin and GC-1 form a complex in photoreceptor cells.
source: Taken together and combined with our finding that the intracellular stability of GC-1 is critically dependent on the presence of rhodopsin, these data demonstrate that rhodopsin and GC-1 form a complex in photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data and the dependency of GC-1 on rhodopsin.

claim: Rhodopsin serves as an interacting partner and a vehicle for ciliary delivery of GC-1.
source: We have found that rhodopsin serves as an interacting partner and a vehicle for ciliary delivery of a key phototransduction protein, GC-1.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: GC-1 is unique in its reliance on rhodopsin, as the other nine proteins tested were expressed in significant amounts and faithfully localized to rod outer segments in the absence of rhodopsin.
source: We further showed that GC-1 is unique in its reliance on rhodopsin, as the other nine proteins tested in this study were expressed in significant amounts and faithfully localized to rod outer segments in the absence of rhodopsin.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figures 1 and 3.

claim: GC-1 delivery requires rhodopsin and can rely on specific targeting information encoded in the rhodopsin molecule.
source: Our study shows that GC-1 delivery requires rhodopsin and, therefore, can rely on specific targeting information encoded in the rhodopsin molecule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimera experiments in Figure 4.

claim: The targeting information in rhodopsin can be replaced by an alternative ciliary targeting sequence from a GPCR not endogenous to photoreceptors.
source: Interestingly, we also found that this information can be replaced by an alternative ciliary targeting sequence from a GPCR not endogenous to photoreceptors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Htr6 chimera experiments in Figure 4.

claim: The functions of binding/stabilization of GC-1 and ciliary targeting are performed by different parts of the rhodopsin molecule.
source: This suggests that the functions of binding/stabilization of GC-1 and ciliary targeting are performed by different parts of the rhodopsin molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the chimera experiments showing that the rhodopsin core is necessary for GC-1 stabilization while the C-terminus can be replaced.

claim: Both rhodopsin and GC-1 utilize IFT for their ciliary trafficking and co-precipitate with IFT proteins.
source: Our findings also shed new light on the report that both rhodopsin and GC-1 utilize IFT for their ciliary trafficking and co-precipitate with IFT proteins (Bhowmick et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is rhodopsin that drives the rhodopsin-GC-1 complex for IFT-mediated ciliary delivery in photoreceptor cells.
source: The authors hypothesized that GC-1 plays a primary role in assembling cargo for the IFT particle bound for ciliary delivery. Our data suggest that it is rhodopsin that drives this complex, at least in photoreceptor cells where these proteins are specifically expressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that GC-1 depends on rhodopsin but not vice versa.

claim: Rhodopsin does not require GC-1 as its expression level and localization remain normal in rods of GC-1 knockout mice.
source: Unlike GC-1's reliance on rhodopsin for its intracellular stability or outer segment trafficking, rhodopsin does not require GC-1 as its expression level and localization remain normal in rods of GC-1 knockout mice (Baehr et al., 2007; and this study).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2 and supported by a citation.

claim: The outer segment trafficking of cone opsins is not affected by the lack of GC-1.
source: The outer segment trafficking of cone opsins is not affected by the lack of GC-1 either (Baehr et al., 2007; Karan et al., 2008), although GC-1 knockout cones undergo rapid degeneration, likely because they do not express GC-2 – an enzyme with redundant function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GC-1 knockout cones undergo rapid degeneration, likely because they do not express GC-2.
source: The outer segment trafficking of cone opsins is not affected by the lack of GC-1 either (Baehr et al., 2007; Karan et al., 2008), although GC-1 knockout cones undergo rapid degeneration, likely because they do not express GC-2 – an enzyme with redundant function.
evidence: This is supported by citations and includes speculative reasoning about the cause of degeneration.

claim: The primary role of rhodopsin in guiding GC-1 to the outer segment is consistent with rhodopsin directly interacting with IFT20.
source: The primary role of rhodopsin in guiding GC-1 to the outer segment is further consistent with rhodopsin directly interacting with IFT20, a mobile component of the IFT complex responsible for recruiting IFT cargo at the Golgi network (Crouse et al., 2014; Keady et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IFT20 is a mobile component of the IFT complex responsible for recruiting IFT cargo at the Golgi network.

claim: GC-1 trafficking requires participation of chaperone proteins, most importantly DnaJB6.

claim: GC-1 interaction with DnaJB6 is transient, most likely in route to the outer segment.
source: Our data suggest that GC-1 interaction with DnaJB6 is transient, most likely in route to the outer segment, since we were not able to co-precipitate DnaJB6 with GC-1 from whole retina lysates (Figure 5).

claim: The majority of GC-1 co-precipitates with rhodopsin from whole retina lysates.
source: In contrast, the majority of GC-1 co-precipitates with rhodopsin from these same lysates, suggesting that these proteins remain in a complex after being delivered to the outer segment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5.

claim: GC-1 and rhodopsin remain in a complex after being delivered to the outer segment.
source: In contrast, the majority of GC-1 co-precipitates with rhodopsin from these same lysates, suggesting that these proteins remain in a complex after being delivered to the outer segment.

claim: The mature GC-1-rhodopsin complex may contain additional protein component(s).
source: Although our data do not exclude that the mature GC-1-rhodopsin complex may contain additional protein component(s), our attempts to identify such components by mass spectrometry have not yielded potential candidates.
